Predictions, plots and derivatives with transformed covariates

Source: vignettes/transformed-covariates.Rmd
transformed-covariates.Rmd

A model fitted with s(log(x)) uses a transformed covariate, but we may want to predict at supplied values of x, plot the result against x, or estimate change per unit of x. This vignette shows how to make those choices while keeping the model’s transformation intact.

We load {gratia} and {mgcv} for the examples:

library("gratia")
load_mgcv()

Fit a count model with a transformed covariate and an effort offset

We simulate independent Poisson counts. The rate per unit of effort varies nonlinearly with log(x), and multiplying that rate by effort gives each observation’s expected count. Thus, twice the effort gives twice the expected count at the same value of x.

set.seed(42)
dat <- data.frame(x = runif(150, 1, 5), effort = runif(150, 1, 3))
dat$y <- rpois(nrow(dat), dat$effort * exp(sin(log(dat$x))))

With a log link, the multiplicative effort term becomes an additive offset(log(effort)). We fit a smooth of log(x) to estimate the remaining variation in the log expected count:

m <- gam(y ~ s(log(x), k = 6) + offset(log(effort)),
  family = poisson(), data = dat, method = "REML")

Predict at values of the original covariates

Supply the original x and effort values when predicting at new observations; gratia evaluates their transformations. Here we hold effort at two units and compare the contribution of the smooth with the complete fitted mean. smooth_estimates() needs only x, whereas fitted_values() also needs the effort offset:

nd <- data.frame(x = seq(1.2, 4.8, length.out = 8), effort = 2)
smooth_estimates(m, data = nd["x"])
#> # A tibble: 8 × 7
#>   .smooth   .type .by   .estimate    .se `log(x)` .gratia_raw_x
#>   <chr>     <chr> <chr>     <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1 s(log(x)) TPRS  NA      -0.544  0.107     0.182          1.2 
#> 2 s(log(x)) TPRS  NA      -0.323  0.0748    0.539          1.71
#> 3 s(log(x)) TPRS  NA      -0.160  0.0543    0.801          2.23
#> 4 s(log(x)) TPRS  NA      -0.0318 0.0428    1.01           2.74
#> 5 s(log(x)) TPRS  NA       0.0747 0.0396    1.18           3.26
#> 6 s(log(x)) TPRS  NA       0.166  0.0425    1.33           3.77
#> 7 s(log(x)) TPRS  NA       0.245  0.0487    1.46           4.29
#> 8 s(log(x)) TPRS  NA       0.315  0.0561    1.57           4.8
fitted_values(m, data = nd)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 8
#>    .row     x effort .parameter .fitted    .se .lower_ci .upper_ci
#>   <int> <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>        <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1     1  1.2       2 mean          2.51 0.107       2.03      3.09
#> 2     2  1.71      2 mean          3.13 0.0748      2.70      3.62
#> 3     3  2.23      2 mean          3.68 0.0543      3.31      4.09
#> 4     4  2.74      2 mean          4.18 0.0428      3.85      4.55
#> 5     5  3.26      2 mean          4.65 0.0396      4.31      5.03
#> 6     6  3.77      2 mean          5.10 0.0425      4.69      5.54
#> 7     7  4.29      2 mean          5.52 0.0487      5.01      6.07
#> 8     8  4.8       2 mean          5.92 0.0561      5.30      6.61

Without supplied prediction data, smooth_estimates() creates an evenly spaced grid on the scale used in the smooth: here, log(x). We can plot the estimated contribution directly on that scale:

sm <- smooth_estimates(m, n = 30)
draw(sm)

If you already have values on the transformed scale, supply a column named exactly as it appears in the model, here log(x):

evaluated <- data.frame(`log(x)` = log(nd$x), check.names = FALSE)
smooth_estimates(m, data = evaluated)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 6
#>   .smooth   .type .by   .estimate    .se `log(x)`
#>   <chr>     <chr> <chr>     <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 s(log(x)) TPRS  NA      -0.544  0.107     0.182
#> 2 s(log(x)) TPRS  NA      -0.323  0.0748    0.539
#> 3 s(log(x)) TPRS  NA      -0.160  0.0543    0.801
#> 4 s(log(x)) TPRS  NA      -0.0318 0.0428    1.01 
#> 5 s(log(x)) TPRS  NA       0.0747 0.0396    1.18 
#> 6 s(log(x)) TPRS  NA       0.166  0.0425    1.33 
#> 7 s(log(x)) TPRS  NA       0.245  0.0487    1.46 
#> 8 s(log(x)) TPRS  NA       0.315  0.0561    1.57

If both x and log(x) are supplied, gratia computes the transformation from x. To build a grid on the original scale, use data_slice() with the original fitting data. The following call creates eight evenly spaced x values while holding effort at two:

data_slice(m, x = evenly(x, n = 8), effort = 2, data = dat)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 2
#>       x effort
#>   <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1  1.00      2
#> 2  1.57      2
#> 3  2.13      2
#> 4  2.70      2
#> 5  3.26      2
#> 6  3.83      2
#> 7  4.39      2
#> 8  4.96      2

Plot against the original covariates

Drawing methods use the model’s covariate coordinates by default. For example, log(x) is plotted against log(x), with a matching axis label, whether it is inside a smooth or a parametric term. Set back_transform = TRUE to display x instead. The estimated smooth contribution remains on the model’s linear predictor scale. The following calls request an axis in the original units, first from the fitted model and then from saved smooth estimates.

draw(m, back_transform = TRUE)

sm_raw <- smooth_estimates(m, back_transform = TRUE)
draw(sm_raw, back_transform = TRUE)

The same option works for transformed covariates in parametric terms. We fit a Poisson model with a linear effect of log(x) and the same effort offset. Plot the effect against log(x) and x, then make the plot in the original units using the output of parametric_effects().

m_parametric <- gam(y ~ log(x) + offset(log(effort)),
  family = poisson(), data = dat)
draw(m_parametric)

draw(m_parametric, back_transform = TRUE)

pe <- parametric_effects(m_parametric)
draw(pe, back_transform = TRUE)

For a surface, back_transform = TRUE changes both displayed axes. To illustrate this, we add an independent covariate z and fit a tensor-product smooth using log(x) and sqrt(z). The simulated counts still depend only on x and effort; z supplies a second axis for this display example:

dat_surface <- transform(dat, z = runif(nrow(dat), 1, 4))

Fit a smooth over the transformed coordinates, then request original-scale axes for both covariates when drawing it.

m_surface <- gam(y ~ te(log(x), sqrt(z)) + offset(log(effort)), family = poisson(),
  data = dat_surface, method = "REML")
draw(m_surface, back_transform = TRUE, contour = FALSE)

back_transform = TRUE also changes where a smooth is evaluated when the grid is generated automatically. For example, consider s(log(x)) with x ranging from 1 to 100. By default, three equally spaced points on the log scale correspond to 1, 10 and 100 in the original units. With smooth_estimates(..., back_transform = TRUE), the same grid size gives 1, 50.5 and 100 in the original units. The smooth is evaluated at the logs of these values. draw(m, back_transform = TRUE) prepares this grid automatically.

Precomputed estimates retain their chosen evaluation points. An object created on a transformed-only grid cannot be drawn on the original scale: its raw coordinates are unavailable. Recompute it with back_transform = TRUE, or supply original covariate values through data when calculating the estimates.

Use your own transformation functions

The transformation need not be named log() or sqrt(). Each smooth axis must depend on one distinct original model covariate, and the transformation must be available when calculating predictions. Here foo() is another name for sqrt(); we supply its environment through envir:

foo <- sqrt
m_foo <- gam(y ~ s(foo(x), k = 6), family = poisson(), data = dat)
sm_foo <- smooth_estimates(m_foo, back_transform = TRUE, envir = environment())
draw(sm_foo, back_transform = TRUE)

Keep the original fitting data and transformation functions available when creating automatic original-scale grids. If the fitting data are unavailable, supply prediction rows in data; if a function or constant is missing, supply its environment in envir. Saved estimates can then be plotted without evaluating the transformation again. Rugs and partial residuals require the original observations and are omitted when those observations cannot be recovered.

Soap-film boundary coordinates are stored on the model scale. A transformed boundary has no retained raw coordinates, so raw-scale drawing raises an error. Draw these soap films with back_transform = FALSE to retain their boundaries.

The old parametric_effects(transform = ...) argument is deprecated. Replace transform = TRUE with back_transform = FALSE, and transform = FALSE with back_transform = TRUE.

Preserve functions defined inside a model-fitting function

A fitted model may retain the formula expression without retaining the local environment in which it was evaluated. In the example below, transform_x() needs the local constant shift. We return the fitted model and that environment together, then use envir when predicting at new observations:

fit_local <- function(dat) {
  shift <- 0.5
  transform_x <- function(x) log(x + shift)
  f <- y ~ s(transform_x(x), k = 6) + offset(log(effort))
  list(model = gam(f, family = poisson(), data = dat, method = "REML"),
    envir = environment(f))
}
bundle <- fit_local(dat)
smooth_estimates(bundle$model, data = nd, envir = bundle$envir)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 7
#>   .smooth           .type .by   .estimate    .se `transform_x(x)` .gratia_raw_x
#>   <chr>             <chr> <chr>     <dbl>  <dbl>            <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1 s(transform_x(x)) TPRS  NA      -0.543  0.113             0.531          1.2 
#> 2 s(transform_x(x)) TPRS  NA      -0.329  0.0772            0.795          1.71
#> 3 s(transform_x(x)) TPRS  NA      -0.164  0.0607            1.00           2.23
#> 4 s(transform_x(x)) TPRS  NA      -0.0295 0.0511            1.18           2.74
#> 5 s(transform_x(x)) TPRS  NA       0.0802 0.0451            1.32           3.26
#> 6 s(transform_x(x)) TPRS  NA       0.170  0.0440            1.45           3.77
#> 7 s(transform_x(x)) TPRS  NA       0.244  0.0497            1.57           4.29
#> 8 s(transform_x(x)) TPRS  NA       0.308  0.0619            1.67           4.8
fitted_values(bundle$model, data = nd, envir = bundle$envir)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 8
#>    .row     x effort .parameter .fitted    .se .lower_ci .upper_ci
#>   <int> <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>        <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1     1  1.2       2 mean          2.51 0.113       2.01      3.13
#> 2     2  1.71      2 mean          3.11 0.0772      2.67      3.62
#> 3     3  2.23      2 mean          3.67 0.0607      3.26      4.13
#> 4     4  2.74      2 mean          4.19 0.0511      3.79      4.64
#> 5     5  3.26      2 mean          4.68 0.0451      4.28      5.11
#> 6     6  3.77      2 mean          5.12 0.0440      4.70      5.58
#> 7     7  4.29      2 mean          5.51 0.0497      5.00      6.08
#> 8     8  4.8       2 mean          5.88 0.0619      5.21      6.64

New predictions require the original definition of transform_x() and the same value of shift. Retaining bundle$envir makes both available after fit_local() has returned.

Choose whether derivatives describe change in x or log(x)

For a contribution f(\log x), the default derivative is with respect to \log x. Set wrt = "covariate" to differentiate with respect to x instead. The latter includes the chain-rule factor 1/x. We compare both derivatives at the prediction rows created earlier. Both describe change in the smooth’s contribution to the log expected count; use response_derivatives() for change in the complete response mean.

derivatives(m, data = nd, type = "central")
#> # A tibble: 8 × 9
#>   .smooth   .by   .fs   .derivative   .se .crit .lower_ci .upper_ci `log(x)`
#>   <chr>     <chr> <chr>       <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 s(log(x)) NA    NA          0.620 0.101  1.96     0.422     0.817    0.182
#> 2 s(log(x)) NA    NA          0.620 0.100  1.96     0.423     0.817    0.539
#> 3 s(log(x)) NA    NA          0.620 0.100  1.96     0.423     0.816    0.801
#> 4 s(log(x)) NA    NA          0.620 0.100  1.96     0.423     0.816    1.01 
#> 5 s(log(x)) NA    NA          0.620 0.100  1.96     0.423     0.816    1.18 
#> 6 s(log(x)) NA    NA          0.620 0.100  1.96     0.423     0.816    1.33 
#> 7 s(log(x)) NA    NA          0.619 0.101  1.96     0.422     0.816    1.46 
#> 8 s(log(x)) NA    NA          0.619 0.101  1.96     0.422     0.817    1.57
derivatives(m, data = nd, type = "central", wrt = "covariate")
#> # A tibble: 8 × 9
#>   .smooth   .by   .fs   .derivative    .se .crit .lower_ci .upper_ci     x
#>   <chr>     <chr> <chr>       <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 s(log(x)) NA    NA          0.516 0.0839  1.96    0.352      0.681  1.2 
#> 2 s(log(x)) NA    NA          0.361 0.0586  1.96    0.247      0.476  1.71
#> 3 s(log(x)) NA    NA          0.278 0.0450  1.96    0.190      0.366  2.23
#> 4 s(log(x)) NA    NA          0.226 0.0366  1.96    0.154      0.298  2.74
#> 5 s(log(x)) NA    NA          0.190 0.0308  1.96    0.130      0.251  3.26
#> 6 s(log(x)) NA    NA          0.164 0.0266  1.96    0.112      0.216  3.77
#> 7 s(log(x)) NA    NA          0.145 0.0235  1.96    0.0986     0.191  4.29
#> 8 s(log(x)) NA    NA          0.129 0.0209  1.96    0.0880     0.170  4.8

Differentiate a surface with respect to one covariate

For a surface, partial_derivatives() varies the coordinate named in focal while holding the other coordinates fixed. wrt chooses the scale of that coordinate. For example, te(log(x), sqrt(z)) represents a contribution f(\log x, \sqrt z), with the following choices:

Arguments Derivative
wrt = "smooth", focal = "log(x)" With respect to \log x, holding \sqrt z fixed
wrt = "covariate", focal = "x" With respect to x, holding z fixed

We simulate a Gaussian response with mean sin(log(x)) * sqrt(z). The positive covariates are sampled independently, and independent Gaussian errors have standard deviation 0.1.

set.seed(43)
tensor_dat <- data.frame(x = runif(150, 1, 5), z = runif(150, 1, 3))
tensor_dat$y <- sin(log(tensor_dat$x)) * sqrt(tensor_dat$z) +
  rnorm(nrow(tensor_dat), sd = 0.1)

We fit a tensor-product smooth using the transformed covariates to estimate that surface:

tensor_model <- gam(y ~ te(log(x), sqrt(z), k = c(4, 4)),
  data = tensor_dat, method = "REML")

Next, we hold z at two and vary x. We calculate derivatives with respect to log(x) and x, then compare the latter with the chain-rule calculation:

# Vary x along a slice with z held fixed.
tensor_nd <- data.frame(x = seq(1.2, 4.8, length.out = 8), z = 2)
pd_smooth <- partial_derivatives(tensor_model, data = tensor_nd,
  wrt = "smooth", focal = "log(x)", type = "central")
pd_covariate <- partial_derivatives(tensor_model, data = tensor_nd,
  wrt = "covariate", focal = "x", type = "central")

# Compare the raw-covariate derivative with the chain-rule calculation.
data.frame(x = tensor_nd$x,
  covariate_derivative = pd_covariate$.partial_deriv,
  smooth_derivative_over_x = pd_smooth$.partial_deriv / tensor_nd$x)
#>          x covariate_derivative smooth_derivative_over_x
#> 1 1.200000           1.10743950               1.10743950
#> 2 1.714286           0.70406919               0.70406919
#> 3 2.228571           0.46255744               0.46255744
#> 4 2.742857           0.30372264               0.30372264
#> 5 3.257143           0.19160164               0.19160164
#> 6 3.771429           0.11442885               0.11442885
#> 7 4.285714           0.07550389               0.07550389
#> 8 4.800000           0.05874753               0.05874753

The first call estimates the derivative from small changes in log(x). The second makes small changes in x and recalculates log(x) before evaluating the smooth. The chain rule gives the relationship \partial f / \partial x = (\partial f / \partial \log x) / x, up to finite-difference approximation error.

For this surface, use focal = "x" or "z" with wrt = "covariate", and supply the original covariate values in data. Keep the other covariate fixed to describe change along a particular slice, as we did with z = 2. The default wrt = "smooth" selects the first numeric smooth coordinate if focal is omitted. Naming it explicitly makes the intended derivative clear. For an untransformed coordinate, such as x in te(x, z), both values of wrt give the same interpretation.

Choosing a finite-difference step

The derivative functions use eps = NULL by default to choose a step from the fitted range of the differentiation coordinate. This is the range of log(x) when differentiating on that smooth coordinate, or of x when using wrt = "covariate". The step therefore follows changes in the covariate’s units and normally stays the same when prediction data are split into batches.

Start with this default. If estimates appear unstable, supply a positive absolute eps in the units of the coordinate being differentiated. For example, eps = 1e-4 with wrt = "covariate" sets the step in units of x. Compare estimates using half and twice the chosen step: very small steps can amplify rounding errors, while large steps give a poorer local approximation. Near a transformation’s domain boundary, choose a step and difference type that keep the evaluation points inside the domain. The FiniteDiff step-size discussion explains this balance.
